title: Validation
content: Validation The global Run verb helpers declare HTTP handlers and attach validation options that parse, transform, and type path parameters, query strings, and request bodies.

title: Verb Helpers
content:
Each verb helper (Run.GET, Run.HEAD, Run.POST, Run.PUT, Run.DELETE, Run.PATCH, Run.OPTIONS, Run.QUERY, and Run.ALL) accepts a handler function or array of functions, with optional validation options first: Export verb helpers by method name in +handler files or as the default export in +middleware files. [!NOTE]
Run is global in route files with no imports needed. See TypeScript.

title: Params and Search
content:
The params and search options validate and transform path parameters and query string values. Without a validator, ctx.params is a string map and ctx.search is a parsed query object (repeated keys become string arrays). A validator is either a function or a Standard Schema (Valibot, Zod, ArkType, etc.): Function validators replace the value with their return value (and reject invalid input by throwing a Response). Standard Schema validators produce a [value, issues] tuple. Validation is lazy: ctx.params and ctx.search run on first property access and cache the result for subsequent reads. [!WARNING]
Standard Schema validators must be synchronous; async schemas throw at runtime.

title: Request Bodies
content:
POST, PUT, PATCH, and QUERY handlers declare body parsing and validation with json or form. When either option configures a validator, ctx.body is a lazy promise for the parsed and validated body; without a validator, ctx.body is undefined (even if size limits are passed; use an identity validator such as json: (value) => value to accept raw parsed data). The body is read and parsed only when ctx.body is awaited (or .then is called), so early rejections avoid reading the request stream. Malformed bodies fail with 400, bodies exceeding configured limits fail with 413, and mismatched Content-Type headers fail with 415. [!NOTE]
ctx.body is a promise, not a function. Read it with await ctx.body; there is nothing to call. [!WARNING]
Calling ctx.request.json() or ctx.request.formData() directly bypasses validation and size limits. Configure json or form on the verb helper and read await ctx.body instead.

title: json
content: Handles application/json requests. Accepts a validator directly or an options object: Option Default Description validator Function or Standard Schema for the parsed JSON maxBytes 1048576 (1MiB) Maximum request body size in bytes

title: form
content: Handles application/x-www-form-urlencoded and multipart/form-data requests. Repeated field names (for both text fields and uploaded files) collapse into arrays. Uploaded multipart files arrive in the parsed record as File instances carrying an extra fieldName property, or as the return value of onFile when provided. Option Default Description validator Function or Standard Schema for the parsed form maxBytes maxFiles * maxFileBytes Maximum request body size in bytes maxParts 1000 Maximum number of parts in a multipart request maxFiles 20 Maximum number of files in a multipart request maxFileBytes 1048576 (1MiB) Maximum size of each uploaded file in bytes onFile (ctx, file) => any called per file; return value replaces file Multipart upload example:

title: Standard Schema
content:
Standard Schema validators resolve to a [value, issues] discriminated tuple: on success, issues is undefined and value has the parsed type; on failure, value holds the raw input and issues lists validation errors. Checking issues narrows value for that read: [!TIP]
Check issues once in the handler and pass narrowed values to the page via next so templates receive validated data directly.

title: Merging Options
content: Options declared across middleware and handlers for the same route merge shallowly: the last validator wins, while object options combine (for example, maxBytes in middleware merges with validator in a handler). Options-only middleware (Run.ALL({ search: ... })) applies shared validation to every nested route.

title: Runtime
content: Runtime At build time, Marko Run compiles route files into a router that creates a context object for each request and passes it through middleware, handlers, and templates. Adapters wire this router into deployment targets automatically, or it can be embedded directly in an existing server.

title: Context
content:
Passed as the first argument (ctx) to middleware and handlers, and available as $global in templates: Property Description route Matched route path pattern string request WHATWG Request for the incoming request method HTTP method string url WHATWG URL for the request signal AbortSignal that aborts on client disconnect ($global.signal) params Path parameters, transformed by any params validator search Query string values, transformed by any search validator body Lazy promise for the validated body when a json or form validator is configured, else undefined data Values passed downstream via next(data) meta Static metadata from +meta platform Adapter-specific platform data parent Calling context for internal ctx.fetch requests, else undefined [!NOTE]
$global.params and $global.url are serialized to the browser by default so client code can read them after resume. Add other properties through ctx.serializedGlobals (see $global.serializedGlobals).

title: fetch
content: Dispatches an internal request through the router using the standard fetch signature. Relative URLs resolve against ctx.url, and the child request's ctx.parent points to the caller's context.

title: render
content: Streams a Marko template as a Response (default status 200, Content-Type: text/html;charset=UTF-8 unless set in init.headers, empty body for HEAD).

title: redirect
content: Returns a redirect response resolving relative paths against ctx.url. Defaults to 302; accepts 301, 302, 303, 307, or 308.

title: back
content: Redirects to the request's Referer header when it shares the same origin as ctx.url, otherwise falls back to fallback (default "/").

title: Typed URLs
content:
Run.href builds URI-encoded URLs checked against the application's routes at compile time when generated types are enabled: Option Description params Values for dynamic segments; required when present; $$ also accepts arrays joined with / search Query string values, typed against the route's search validator when declared hash Fragment appended after # [!NOTE]
In client builds, Marko Run compiles direct Run.href(...) calls away when statically analyzable. Call Run.href directly in browser code rather than aliasing or destructuring Run.

title: router.fetch
content:
Executes the matched route for a WHATWG Request with platform exposed as ctx.platform. Returns: a WHATWG Response from the matched route undefined if the route exited unhandled (throw null) a 404 response if no route matched a 500 response if an uncaught error occurred [!TIP]
For Express and Connect-style Node.js servers, the Node adapter's middleware handles request/response conversion automatically.

title: router.match
content: Synchronously matches an HTTP method and pathname, returning a RouteMatch (params, meta, path, handler, options) or null when unmatched.

content: Executes a RouteMatch returned by router.match (passing null triggers 404 handling), letting custom middleware inspect route metadata between matching and invocation:

title: Getting Started
content: Getting Started Marko Run (@marko/run) is the official application framework for Marko. It turns a directory of templates into a web application with file-based routing, nested layouts, middleware, streaming SSR, and platform adapters. Powered by Vite, Marko Run ships with a default Vite config and Node adapter so a single src/routes/+page.marko file is enough to start serving requests.

title: Using a Template
content: Scaffold a new project with npm init marko: Available starter templates (from marko-js/examples): basic (Marko Run starter), app (full Marko Run app with styling and tests), library (component library), and vite-express (custom Express + @marko/vite). Non-interactive environments accept defaults automatically; pass -t <template>, -n / --name <dir>, -y / --yes, --no-install, or --no-git to configure scaffolding directly.

title: Manual Setup
content:
Marko Run requires only @marko/run alongside marko: Install the package: Create src/routes/+page.marko: Start the development server with the CLI: The server listens at http://localhost:3000. [!NOTE]
Installed adapters are discovered automatically by package name. Add a vite.config.ts only when customizing plugin options or registering additional Vite plugins (see Vite Plugin).

title: File-based Routing
content:
File-based Routing Marko Run maps the directory tree under ./src/routes to URL paths using a small set of +-prefixed filenames. [!NOTE]
Only +-prefixed files are treated as routes. Components, tests, stories, and utilities without a + prefix can live beside the routes that use them without becoming endpoints.

title: +page.marko
content: Defines the page rendered at the directory's path for GET and HEAD requests (and for POST or QUERY requests when a handler invokes next()). At most one page may exist per served path.

title: +layout.marko
content: Wraps all nested layouts and pages under its directory. Layouts are standard Marko components receiving input.content (the nested layout or page) and the request context as $global:

title: +handler.*
content:
Handles HTTP requests at the directory's path via named exports for any HTTP verb: GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, OPTIONS, or QUERY. Each export may be a handler function, an array of handler functions, or a promise resolving to either. At most one handler file (.js or .ts) may exist per served path. Create handlers with the global verb helpers (Run.GET, Run.POST, etc.) for typed validation and data loading: Handlers receive (ctx, next): ctx: the request context (WHATWG Request, params, search, body, data, meta, url, signal; see Context) next: renders the page for GET, POST, and QUERY requests (returning 200 with an empty body for HEAD when a page exists, or 204 when there is no page or for other verbs). Pass an object to next(data) to load data for downstream handlers and pages. [!TIP]
Configure json or form validation and read await ctx.body rather than calling ctx.request.json() or ctx.request.formData(), which bypasses validation and size limits. A handler may return (or throw) a Response, return undefined (which invokes next() automatically), return null (falling through to 404), or throw null (exiting the router as unhandled so downstream server middleware can take over): [!NOTE]
When no HEAD export exists, HEAD requests run the GET handler (or page) with the response body stripped.

title: +middleware.*
content:
Runs before nested middleware and handlers in its directory subtree. Middleware uses a default export accepting the same shapes as handler exports (function, array, or promise) created with Run.ALL or a verb helper. An options-only call such as Run.ALL({ search: ... }) attaches shared validation without adding handler logic: [!NOTE]
Run.ALL(...) middleware runs for every HTTP method; verb-specific middleware runs only for that verb (Run.GET(...) middleware also runs for HEAD).

title: +meta.*
content: Attaches static metadata to a route, exposed as ctx.meta (JSON files or a JS/TS module's default export). When the metadata is an object, top-level keys matching an HTTP verb (GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, OPTIONS, QUERY) whose value is an object are shallowly merged into the base object for that method and excluded from all other methods (non-object verb values are ignored): With this +meta.json, ctx.meta resolves as follows: POST: GET: PUT and all other methods:

title: Special Files
content: Defined only at the top level of the routes directory (src/routes/). Special pages are wrapped by the root +layout.marko (root +middleware.* does not run for them).

title: +404.marko
content: Renders with status 404 when the Accept header includes text/html and no route handled the request.

title: +500.marko
content: Renders with status 500 when the Accept header includes text/html and an uncaught error occurs. Receives input.error (unknown).

title: Static Assets
content: Files served at fixed URLs (such as /favicon.png or /robots.txt) belong in the project's public/ directory (Vite's publicDir), not src/routes/. Files in public/ are copied directly into dist/public/ at build time and served from / by the default server.

title: Execution Order
content:
Given: A request to /about runs in order: Middleware from root to leaf Route handler Layouts from root to leaf Page [!NOTE]
Layouts and pages combine into a single template at build time, adding zero runtime nesting overhead.

title: Path Structure
content: Directory names under src/routes/ fall into four kinds:

title: Static Directories
content: Any ordinary directory name contributes that literal segment to the URL:

title: Pathless Directories
content: Names starting with _ group routes, layouts, or middleware without adding a URL segment:

title: Dynamic Directories
content: Names starting with $ match a single path segment and capture its value in ctx.params. A bare $ matches one segment without capturing it:

title: Catch-all Directories
content: Names starting with $$ match the remainder of the path and capture it in ctx.params; bare $$ matches without capturing. Catch-all directories can also build 404 routes at any level, including the root. Nested routes inside a catch-all directory are not supported:

title: Flat Routes
content: Flat routes encode path segments in file or directory names using . as a separator (anything before + in a routable filename is parsed with the same static, pathless, dynamic, and catch-all rules). Directory-based and flat layouts can be mixed freely and merge into the same route tree. These two structures both define /projects/$projectId/members with root and project layouts: Shared prefixes can also stay in a flat directory:

title: Multiple Paths
content: Separate multiple paths with , so one file serves several routes (/projects/$projectId/members and /projects/$projectId/people):

title: Groups
content: Parentheses group alternating sub-paths within a single flat filename (and may be nested):

title: Optional Segments
content: Pair a segment with an empty or pathless alternative to make it optional (matching both /projects and /projects/home): An empty alternative behaves like defining the file at the parent directory, while a pathless alternative isolates middleware and layouts like a pathless directory.

title: Escaping Characters
content: Wrap control characters (., ,, +, (, ), $, _) in backticks (`) to match them literally in a URL, such as /sitemap.xml: Or escape individual characters:

title: Data Loading
content: Data Loading Handlers and middleware pass server-side data (database queries, sessions, API calls) downstream to nested handlers, layouts, and pages by passing an object to next(data).

title: Passing Data
content:
Values passed to next are shallowly merged into ctx.data, exposed in templates as $global.data: Root middleware can load shared data (such as the current session) while route handlers add route-specific entries. With generated types, $global.data is typed per route and verb based on the middleware and handlers that actually execute before the template. [!WARNING]
Merging is shallow: passing { user: ... } replaces any upstream user entry rather than deep-merging it.

title: Promises over Awaiting
content:
Passing promises through next and unwrapping them in templates with <await> lets responses stream immediately. Static markup and <head> assets reach the browser while data loads, and independent promises resolve in parallel rather than serially. [!WARNING]
Awaiting data in a GET handler before calling next() blocks the entire response until that promise settles, forfeiting streaming for the whole page.

title: Rendering and Responses
content:
next() renders the page for GET, POST, and QUERY requests when a +page.marko exists, returns 200 (empty body) for HEAD when a page exists, and returns 204 when there is no page or for other verbs. Handlers can short-circuit with their own response before calling next(): [!NOTE]
A handler that always returns its own Response never renders the page, so its verb is excluded from the template's generated context union.

title: Forms
content:
When a route has both a +page.marko and a POST handler, respond with one of two patterns depending on the outcome: On success, call ctx.redirect(url, 303) (Post/Redirect/Get) so the browser lands on a GET page that can be refreshed, bookmarked, or shared safely. For validation errors or ephemeral responses, return next({ issues }) to re-render the page inline with feedback while preserving form context. [!WARNING]
Returning next() from a POST produces a POST response, so refreshing the browser prompts to resubmit. Always redirect after a successful state-changing submission.

title: Adapters
content: Adapters Adapters tailor Marko Run's dev server, build output, and preview process to a target runtime or deployment platform. Application routes stay written in Web standard APIs, so swapping the adapter moves the same app across Node.js, Cloudflare Workers, Vercel, Netlify, or static files.

title: Choosing an Adapter

Pass it explicitly in vite.config.ts only to configure options or choose among multiple installed adapters:

title: Node
content: @marko/run-adapter-node deploys Marko Run apps on Node.js and provides Connect/Express-compatible middleware for embedding inside an existing server: routerMiddleware(options?) handles matching routes end to end (options accepts origin, trustProxy, and createPlatform): To inspect matched route metadata before invoking the route, pair matchMiddleware() with invokeMiddleware(options?):

title: Static
content: @marko/run-adapter-static pre-renders routes to static HTML files for any file server or CDN: During build, the adapter renders every static route and crawls same-origin <a> (excluding download and nofollow/enclosure/external), qualifying <link>, and <iframe> references. Use urls (an array or async function receiving discovered routes) to add extra entry points: Each crawled route writes HTML files matching trailingSlashes (default RedirectWithout). For /about: Value Without trailing slash With trailing slash RedirectWithout about.html about/index.html (redirecting to /about when linked as /about/) RedirectWith about.html (redirecting to /about/) about/index.html RewriteWithout about.html about.html (when the host serves it for /about/) RewriteWith about/index.html (when the host serves it for /about) about/index.html Hosts that only resolve directory index files (about/index.html) pair best with RedirectWith or RewriteWith.

title: Cloudflare
content: @marko/run-adapter-cloudflare runs routes inside Cloudflare Workers (workerd during dev via @cloudflare/vite-plugin) and builds a Worker bundle ready for wrangler deploy: The adapter defaults compatibility_date, nodejs_compat, and an ASSETS binding automatically when no wrangler.jsonc / wrangler.toml overrides them, and types ctx.platform as CloudflarePlatformInfo. Local marko-run preview uses wrangler dev against the built Worker output.

title: Vercel
content: @marko/run-adapter-vercel emits a Vercel Build Output API v3 bundle under .vercel/output with streaming Node.js Functions and types ctx.platform as VercelPlatformInfo: Optional function settings (runtime, regions, memory, maxDuration) can be passed to the adapter in vite.config.ts:

title: Netlify
content: @marko/run-adapter-netlify deploys to Netlify Functions or Edge Functions (marko-run preview requires netlify-cli): Configure netlify.toml for Netlify Functions: For Edge Functions, pass edge: true in vite.config.ts and set edge_functions in netlify.toml:

content: An adapter implements the Adapter interface from @marko/run/vite with hooks for dev, build, and preview. See the official adapters as reference implementations.

title: Why Marko?
content: Why Marko? Marko builds fast, maintainable web applications by evolving HTML directly rather than replacing it with JavaScript abstractions. Its architecture resolves three core web development tradeoffs at compile time.

title: HTML Can't Scale
content: HTML was built for static documents, not coordinated application state. Updating several parts of a page from one interaction requires manual DOM bookkeeping across elements: Every new element that depends on cart state adds another imperative update site.

title: Component Coordination
content: Platform primitives like Custom Elements encapsulate markup and styles, but still require imperative wiring and boilerplate for basic interaction: Sharing state across multiple custom elements forces manual pub-sub buses, subscription cleanup in connectedCallback / disconnectedCallback, and imperative .open() / .close() APIs that resist declarative composition.

title: Runtime Burden
content: When template analysis, dependency tracking, and virtual tree diffing happen at runtime, every user session repeats work that is static at build time: On the client, browsers download component trees for static markup, re-execute templates during hydration, and maintain runtime dependency graphs just to update a few dynamic nodes. On the server, building an intermediate tree before serializing to HTML allocates memory and delays the first byte on every request. Moving static analysis from runtime to compile time eliminates work for both servers and browsers.

title: Augment HTML
content: Marko extends HTML directly so templates grow from static markup to dynamic, asynchronous interfaces without switching paradigms. Static HTML works as a Marko template: Control flow integrates directly into markup: Async rendering, placeholders, and error boundaries follow the same tag syntax:

title: Component Encapsulation
content: Components colocate markup, scoped styles, and reactive state in a single .marko file with declarative inputs and no imperative setup: Interactive components coordinate state across elements through reactive declarations rather than manual subscriptions:

title: Compile-Time Intelligence
content: Analyzing templates at build time lets Marko generate output tailored to each runtime environment. Only interactive expressions ship JavaScript to the browser; static markup renders on the server and contributes zero bytes to the client bundle: Dependency graphs resolve at build time rather than runtime: When firstName updates, compiled code updates only the dependent fullName, heading text, and initials without diffing the rest of the template. Server builds concatenate HTML strings directly into a stream; browser builds emit surgical DOM updates and deserialize only the state needed for interactivity.

title: The Result
content: Shifting complexity to the compiler makes performance the default outcome. Pages stream HTML immediately, ship JavaScript proportional to interactivity rather than template size, and update affected DOM nodes directly. Because components colocate markup, styling, and state with full TypeScript checking, code stays modular as applications grow, and uncontrolled components can adopt parent control through controllable patterns without rewriting their internals.

title: Welcome to Marko!
content: Welcome to Marko! Marko is a declarative, HTML-based language designed for fast, maintainable web applications.

title: Beyond Vanilla HTML
content: Plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript excel at static documents, but complex interfaces expose three structural limits: imperative DOM updates tangle state with presentation, global CSS creates naming collisions, and manual DOM coordination degrades both maintainability and performance as features grow. Marko addresses these limits by extending HTML itself with components, reactive state, and compile-time optimization.

title: Declarative Language
content: Marko templates describe what the interface renders for a given state rather than the imperative steps to mutate the DOM.

title: Components
content: Every .marko file is a reusable component that composes like a native HTML tag.

title: State Management
content: State lives directly in markup through tag variables. Reassigning state propagates updates automatically, while event handlers and <script> blocks handle side effects.

title: Performance-First Architecture
content: Marko shifts framework overhead from the browser to the build step.

title: Targeted Compilation
content: Each template compiles twice: once for the server and once for the browser. Server output concatenates strings directly into an HTML stream for maximum throughput; browser output targets bundle size and ships code only for expressions that can change on the client.

title: Fine-Grained Reactivity
content: The compiler traces dependencies between state and DOM nodes at build time. When state changes, the browser updates only the affected nodes with no virtual DOM diffing or runtime dependency tracking.

title: Streaming
content: Marko streams HTML to the browser as chunks become ready. Both in-order and out-of-order streaming are built into the language with <await> and <try>.

title: Resumability
content: Alongside streamed HTML, Marko serializes only the state needed for interactivity. The browser attaches event listeners and resumes from the server-rendered DOM without re-executing component setup or re-rendering templates.

title: The Marko Mindset
content: Write declarative HTML first, introduce state and components where needed, and let the compiler handle server streaming, code splitting, and DOM updates.

title: Getting Started
content:
Getting Started [!NOTE]
This documentation covers Marko 6 and the Tags API. For Marko 5, use the version selector in the bottom left or visit v5.markojs.com. Marko reimagines HTML as a declarative language for dynamic, reactive web applications. Nearly any valid HTML is valid Marko, extended with components, control flow, and compiled reactivity.

title: Prerequisite Knowledge
content: Marko builds directly on core web standards, so familiarity with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript carries straight over. For foundational web guides, see MDN and freeCodeCamp.

title: Next Steps
content: Installation Welcome to Marko Marko Fundamentals

title: Styling
content: Styling Marko integrates CSS directly into components through inline <style> tags, auto-discovered stylesheets, CSS Modules, and explicit imports.

title: Inline Styles
content: Marko enhances <style> so styles are extracted, deduplicated, and optimized by the project's bundler. A template may include any number of <style> tags. By default, styles are globally scoped. Projects using global styles often follow a naming convention such as BEM to prevent collisions. Append a file extension to <style> to use CSS preprocessors such as SCSS or Less:

title: Inline CSS Modules
content: Adding a tag variable to <style> compiles it as a CSS Module, scoping class names automatically and exposing the class map as an object: File extensions combine with CSS Modules for preprocessor support:

title: Dynamic Values
content:
A <style> tag accepts ${...} interpolations so reactive values can live alongside static rules: The stylesheet is still extracted and bundled once. Each interpolation compiles to a CSS custom property updated by Marko as state changes. [!NOTE]
Dynamic values work only in CSS declaration value positions and apply to subsequent sibling elements and their descendants. See <style> Dynamic Values for details.

title: Per-Item Values
content:
Because dynamic values apply to the siblings following each <style> tag, placing one inside a <for> scopes the interpolated values to each iteration: [!WARNING]
Each iteration renders a <style> element among the items, so :nth-child counts those elements and misses its targets. Use :nth-of-type instead, which counts only elements of the same tag.

title: Auto-Discovered Styles
content:
A stylesheet adjacent to any .marko template is discovered automatically and bundled identically to an inline <style>. Name it style.<ext> next to index.marko, or <name>.style.<ext> next to <name>.marko. [!TIP]
Moving styles into an adjacent file keeps large templates concise without adding explicit imports.

title: Imported Styles
content: Stylesheets can also be imported explicitly, which is useful when sharing styles across templates:

title: Imported CSS Modules
content:
External CSS Module files (*.module.css) export their class map as the default export: [!NOTE]
Vite and most modern bundlers support *.module.css out of the box.

title: Publishing Components
content: Publishing Components Marko component libraries distribute .marko templates, compiled type declarations, and styles as standard npm packages discovered through marko.json.

title: Package Configuration
content: Place a marko.json at the package root pointing "exports" to the directory of public tags: When package.json defines an "exports" map, it must expose that same on-disk directory because compiled consumer templates import discovered tags directly by package path (for example @acme/ui/dist/tags/acme-icon/index.marko): Prefix exported tag names (such as acme-button) to avoid collisions with other libraries. Place internal helper tags inside a nested tags/ directory (such as dist/tags/tags/) so only the library itself can resolve them.

title: Building Declarations
content: Run mtc (@marko/type-check) to emit type-stripped .marko files alongside .d.marko.ts declaration files into dist/. Consumers get full autocomplete and type checking without requiring TypeScript compilation of node_modules. See the library starter for a complete build and CSS pipeline setup.

title: Storybook
content: Preview and document library components with @storybook/marko and @storybook/marko-vite, which build stories using @marko/vite in browser mode.

title: Marko 5 Interop
content: Marko 5 Interop [!TLDR] marko@6 is not backward compatible with the Class API marko@5 is forward compatible and runs both Class and Tags APIs together In Marko 5, per-file heuristics select which runtime compiles each template Marko 5 uses the Class API, while Marko 6 uses the Tags API. Because Marko 6 has removed the Class API, incremental migrations run on Marko 5 at the project root, which ships an interoperable layer for both runtimes. Because the two runtimes are distinct, minimize crossing between them by grouping Tags API components so they primarily render other Tags API components.

title: API Heuristics
content: In Marko 5, the compiler classifies each .marko file as a whole using the heuristics below. Every feature in a single file must belong to the same API; mixing Class API and Tags API syntax in one file is not allowed, and an opt-in comment cannot override conflicting syntax.

title: Directory Name
content: Marko 5 discovers Class API tags in components/ directories, while Marko 6 discovers Tags API tags in tags/ directories. Files inside a tags/ directory compile with the Tags API. Two exceptions apply: files inside a components/ directory nested under tags/ do not inherit the tags/ rule (so they fall through to the remaining heuristics, allowing vendored Class API components inside a tags/ tree), and directories registered through a marko.json tags-dir are unaffected by this rule.

title: Comment Opt-In
content:
A comment matching use class or use tags in a template, tag, or attribute-tag body explicitly selects the API for that file: Any Marko comment form (//, /* */, or <!-- -->) works in those body positions; comments inside opening tags or inside <script>/static blocks are ignored. [!TIP]
Explicit opt-ins are only needed when a file sits outside tags/ and contains no API-specific syntax, such as an ambiguous Marko Run +page.marko or +layout.marko.

title: Class API Syntax
content:
An otherwise ambiguous file compiles as Class API if it contains: A class {} block A style {} block Inline JS in a $ scriptlet; An attribute argument (<button onClick("handleClick")>) Any of these Class API tags (see getFeatureTypeFromCoreTagName in feature-detection.ts): <await-reorderer>, <class>, <include-html>, <include-text>, <init-components>, <macro>, <module-code>, or <while> [!NOTE]
static, server, and client statements work in both APIs and are not detection signals.

title: Tags API Syntax
content: An otherwise ambiguous file compiles as Tags API if it contains: A tag variable (<div/var>) The bind shorthand (:=) Any of these Tags API tags (see getFeatureTypeFromCoreTagName in feature-detection.ts): <const>, <debug>, <define>, <id>, <let>, <lifecycle>, <log>, <return>, <show>, or <try>

title: Exclusive Tag Library
content: If an ambiguous file discovers tags exclusively in tags/ directories with no components/ directories in scope, it defaults to the Tags API: If any components/ directory is in scope, ambiguous files default to the Class API unless marked with a // use tags comment or Tags API syntax:

title: Limitations
content: Attributes, content, attribute tags, and tag parameters all pass across the Class/Tags boundary. Pending promises do not: keep each <await> and the content it renders within a single API rather than passing unsettled <await> content across the boundary.

title: Low-Level APIs
content: Low-Level APIs Marko's compiler exposes programmatic compilation and tag-library hooks for tooling, bundler plugins, and custom syntax extensions. Standard application code should rely on core tags and custom tags directly.

title: Compiler API
content: Use @marko/compiler to compile .marko templates programmatically into server HTML modules, browser DOM modules, or Babel ASTs, and to wire virtual dependencies and asset manifests into custom build tools.

title: Taglib Hooks
content: A tag library's marko.json can register Babel-based migrators (run when output: "migrate" or before translation) and translators (run during HTML/DOM code generation) for custom tags. Register custom libraries programmatically via compiler.taglib.register (see Tag Libraries) or ship a marko.json at a package root.

title: Library Integration
content: Library Integration Marko integrates with imperative JavaScript libraries and Web Components through <lifecycle>, element references, marko.json tag registration, and Template.mount.

title: Imperative Libraries
content: Use <lifecycle> with a client import and a native element reference to initialize, update, and tear down third-party DOM widgets: Any reactive value read in the <lifecycle> attributes triggers onUpdate automatically, while onMount and onDestroy run once when the template mounts and unmounts in the browser.

title: Custom Elements
content: Declare a custom element as an HTML tag in marko.json so the compiler emits it verbatim (see Custom Tags and TypeScript): Marko writes attributes on registered custom elements with setAttribute, never as JavaScript properties. When a custom element exposes a property-only API (such as complex object inputs), set it through an element reference inside <script>: For non-lowercase custom events, attach listeners with the on- prefix (on-dateSelected) so event name casing is preserved.

title: Mounting Marko
content:
To embed a Marko template inside a non-Marko application or custom element, mount it into a light DOM Element with Template.mount: [!NOTE]
Template.mount requires an HTML Element in the light DOM. Marko delegates events on document and inherits the parent element's HTML namespace, so mounting inside a ShadowRoot or DocumentFragment is not supported.

title: Duplicate Form Submissions
content: Duplicate Form Submissions Guard forms against repeated clicks and network retries by tracking in-flight submission state on the client and redirecting after successful server writes.

title: Client Guard
content: Track submission state with <let> and disable the submit button while an async request is in flight: Checking if (submitting) return; inside onSubmit prevents duplicate submissions triggered via the keyboard even before the disabled state paints, and resetting submitting in finally restores the form if the request fails.

title: Server Redirect
content: For standard HTML POST forms handled by Marko Run, respond to successful mutations with a redirect (303 See Other) using ctx.redirect("/orders/complete", 303). This implements Post/Redirect/Get so browser refreshes and back-button navigations replay a safe GET instead of resubmitting the form.

title: Why is Marko Fast?
content: Why is Marko Fast? [!TLDR] Zero-JS by default with fine-grained bundling Targeted compilation for server and browser First-class HTML streaming Compile-time reactivity and resumability Marko achieves tiny client bundles, high-throughput SSR (1, 2), and fast DOM updates by moving work out of runtime JavaScript and into the compiler. Five architectural decisions drive this performance.

title: Targeted Compilation
content: The compiler generates two separate outputs per template: one for the server and one for the browser (inspect both live in the Playground under "Server JS" and "Client JS").

title: Server Compilation
content: Virtual DOM renderers build an in-memory tree first and serialize it to HTML in a second pass. Marko compiles templates into single-pass string concatenation writing straight to an HTML stream, eliminating intermediate tree allocations and enabling HTML streaming natively.

title: Client Compilation
content: After fine-grained bundling, browser output includes only serialized state, event handlers, <script> effects, and a tree-shaken subset of runtime helpers. Compile-time reactivity removes the need for a JavaScript DOM mirror.

title: Runtime Coordination
content: Server HTML embeds compact markers and serialized state. Browser code reads those markers to resume directly from the existing DOM without re-executing server work. See Targeted Compilation.

title: HTML Streaming
content: Marko flushes HTML to the browser as chunks finish rendering rather than buffering the whole page: Marko has supported HTML streaming since 2014. See HTML Streaming.

title: JS Scales from Zero
content: Static markup compiles to zero browser JavaScript even inside the same template as interactive controls, and server work is never re-run in the browser.

title: Fine-Grained Bundling
content: The compiler analyzes templates at the expression level rather than component-level islands: When server-rendered, the browser receives only the two click handlers and the <span> text update; none of the product heading, description, or price rendering logic ships to the client. See Fine-Grained Bundling.

title: Resumability
content: Traditional SSR relies on hydration, re-executing component code in the browser to recreate state and wire listeners. Marko skips hydration: client code deserializes only needed state, attaches delegated listeners, and locates target DOM nodes directly via server markers.

title: Tree-Shakeable Runtime
content: Compiled templates import only the specific runtime helpers they use: Bundlers tree-shake unused helpers away so unused language features add zero bytes.

title: Compile-Time Reactivity
content: Dependency graphs resolve at compile time: The compiler emits a pre-computed update sequence for count that recalculates doubled and updates both text nodes directly, with no runtime dependency tracking.

title: Performance by Default
content: Marko's language design makes fast patterns the natural path (the pit of success): async rendering streams automatically, static expressions stay on the server without annotations, and reactive updates are compiled ahead of time. Refined in production since 2014, these architectural choices keep both SSR latency and browser bundles lean as applications grow.

title: Further Reading
content: Why Marko? Targeted Compilation Fine-Grained Bundling HTML Streaming

title: Targeted Compilation
content: Targeted Compilation [!TLDR] Marko compiles every template separately for server and browser environments Server output concatenates strings directly into an HTML stream Client output generates surgical DOM updates for interactive expressions only Server-side rendering and client-side interactivity have fundamentally different performance constraints. Rather than running one runtime in both places, Marko compiles each template into two specialized outputs tailored to its target environment.

title: Server Compilation
content: On the server, templates compile to direct string concatenation written into an HTML stream, avoiding DOM or virtual tree allocation altogether: Static markup is pre-concatenated at build time, dynamic values are escaped inline, and conditionals compile to direct branches integrated with HTML streaming.

title: Client Compilation
content: In the browser, templates compile to direct DOM updates scoped strictly to interactive expressions: When this component renders on the server, the browser bundle contains only the liked state, click handler, and update code for the button's class and text. Static markup such as ${input.title} produces zero client JavaScript.

title: Environment Coordination
content: Server and browser outputs coordinate seamlessly through fine-grained bundling and serialized resume markers: Server output renders the complete HTML document, including the heading and all tab panels. When server-rendered, client output ships only the tab-switching handler and aria-selected / hidden updates, with no code for creating the heading or tab bodies.

title: Benefits
content: Templates are authored once while each environment executes code shaped for its workload: single-pass string streaming on the server, and direct DOM updates with zero unused rendering logic in the browser. Because client bundles grow only with interactivity rather than total markup, pages stay lean as applications scale while keeping progressive enhancement intact by default.

title: HTML Streaming
content: HTML Streaming [!TLDR] HTML streaming sends markup to the browser incrementally as chunks become ready <await> and <try> enable in-order and out-of-order streaming declaratively Built-in placeholders and error boundaries handle loading and failure states Marko streams HTML incrementally as templates render rather than buffering the entire document before sending the first byte. Using <await> and <try>, templates flush static markup and <head> assets immediately while slow data fetches resolve in parallel.

title: Background
content: Browsers have rendered partial HTML progressively since 1994, and HTTP has supported streaming responses since HTTP/1.1 chunked transfer encoding (1999) and HTTP/2–HTTP/3 framing. Marko has shipped native HTML streaming since 2014.

title: Streaming Modes
content: In in-order streaming, HTML chunks arrive in exact document order, pausing at each pending <await> until it resolves. In out-of-order streaming, placing <await> inside <try> with <@placeholder> flushes the placeholder immediately and streams the resolved HTML later with a tiny inline script that swaps it into place.

title: Perceived Performance
content: Users see navigation, layout, and critical content immediately instead of staring at a blank screen while slow queries finish.

title: Network Performance
content: Streaming delivers faster Time to First Byte (TTFB) so browsers begin parsing <head> immediately, triggers earlier downloads for stylesheets, fonts, and scripts while server data is still loading, and improves Time to Interactive (TTI) by letting visible interactive regions resume as soon as their chunks arrive.

title: Reduced Server Load
content: Flushing HTML incrementally avoids holding full rendered documents in server memory, lowering peak memory usage and improving throughput.

title: <await>
content: Waits for a promise and renders its resolved value through a tag parameter: Marko flushes all HTML preceding <await> immediately, then flushes the resolved body and trailing HTML once getUser() resolves.

title: <try>
content: Wraps async sections with loading placeholders and error boundaries: @placeholder Renders immediately while nested <await> promises are pending, opting into out-of-order streaming. Resolved chunks stream as soon as ready regardless of document order and swap into the placeholder's position on the client. @catch Catches errors thrown while rendering <try> content (including rejected <await> promises) and renders fallback markup without aborting the rest of the page.

title: Layout Shift
content: Replacing a placeholder with differently sized content can shift surrounding elements (CLS): Size placeholders or skeleton screens to match the resolved content's dimensions. Fall back to in-order streaming (omit @placeholder) when the resolved height is unpredictable and sits above the fold.

title: Avoiding Buffering
content: Some proxies, CDNs, and compressors buffer responses by default, hiding streaming benefits until tuned. Reverse Proxies Disable proxy buffering (or lower buffer sizes). Use HTTP/1.1 or higher for upstream connections (HTTP/1.0 does not support chunked streaming). Enable upstream keep-alive to avoid connection setup latency. For latency-critical small chunks: reduce gzip/brotli buffer sizes, tune TLS record sizes, and send X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff so browsers do not buffer initial bytes for MIME sniffing. NGINX Configure NGINX's http_proxy module: Apache Apache streams by default; if a host overrides it, check mod_proxy and its environment variables. CDNs Fastly (Varnish) Ensure VCL sets beresp.do_stream = true. Akamai Features like Adaptive Acceleration, Ion, mPulse, or Prefetch can buffer chunked responses. Disable response buffering in configuration: Node.js Compression When compressing small HTML chunks in Node.js, configure Z_PARTIAL_FLUSH on zlib.createGzip: pipe() invokes flush() on the target stream after every chunk so compressed data reaches the client without waiting for a full compression buffer.

title: Serializable State
content: Serializable State [!TLDR] Marko serializes only state that browser code reads so pages resume without re-rendering Most JavaScript and Web API built-ins, promises, symbols, and cyclic references are supported Template-authored functions and closures serialize; external module functions, custom classes, and DOM nodes do not To resume server-rendered HTML in the browser, Marko serializes only the server values referenced by client event handlers, <script> effects, and reactive updates.

title: Supported Types
content: Marko's serializer supports most standard JavaScript and Web API data types: Primitives: undefined, null, boolean, number, string, bigint Plain objects and arrays containing serializable values Date, RegExp, Map, Set Typed arrays, ArrayBuffer, and DataView Promise, generators, async generators, and ReadableStream URL, URLSearchParams, Headers, Request, Response, and FormData (string entries) Built-in Error types, including AggregateError Intl formatters and Temporal values Symbols (well-known, registered, and unregistered Symbol()) Functions and closures authored inside .marko templates (and supported JS built-in functions) For the exact list, see serializer.ts. Reactive state reaches the client automatically when browser code depends on it. $global stays server-only unless properties are listed in $global.serializedGlobals so request-scoped values such as a locale can be read after resume.

title: Shared References
content: Because Marko serializes to JavaScript rather than JSON, a value reached multiple times is written once and referenced everywhere else. Object identity carries across server and browser, and cyclic graphs restore intact. Consider a comment list where several comments share one author object: Every comment by the same author points to the same deserialized record, so comment.author === muted matches without comparing IDs. Reference sharing also persists across streaming flushes when later chunks refer back to objects sent in earlier chunks.

title: Unserializable Data
content: Values that cannot be serialized across the server-to-client boundary include: Functions imported from external .js or .ts modules, or created dynamically outside .marko templates Custom class instances (keep plain data in state and instantiate classes on the client inside <lifecycle> or <script>) DOM nodes and elements (use native element references instead) Functions and closures defined directly inside .marko templates are compiler-registered and serializable: Keep reactive state as plain serializable data rather than custom class instances or DOM references:

title: Separation of Concerns
content: Separation of Concerns [!TLDR] Separating files by technology (HTML, CSS, JS) splits single features across multiple files Co-locating markup, scoped styles, and behavior separates code by functional concern instead Component boundaries align with feature and domain responsibilities rather than file extensions Co-locating markup, styling, and reactive logic inside a single .marko file often raises a question: does this violate separation of concerns? The principle argues for separating distinct responsibilities, not separating programming languages.

title: Technology vs. Functionality
content: Consider a modal dialog organized by file extension: This layout separates technologies, not concerns. Every real concern of the modal (open/close state, backdrop layout, keyboard Escape handling, focus management) cuts across HTML, CSS, and JavaScript at once. Adding a single behavior such as closing on Escape or clicking outside forces coordinated edits across all three files, invites orphaned CSS selectors and stale DOM IDs, and fragments the mental model of one feature.

title: Organizing by Feature
content: In Marko, a component groups everything required for one piece of functionality into a single file, using CSS Modules (<style/styles>) when class names should be scoped to the component: State, markup, event handling, and scoped styles live together and move together when refactored or reused.

title: Drawing Boundaries
content: Marko lets applications draw boundaries along functional lines (components, features, domains, and lower-level utilities) and adjust them as requirements evolve. For example, an inline formatted phone input inside a form: can be extracted into a dedicated component once it grows or is needed elsewhere, with zero bundle penalty thanks to fine-grained bundling:

title: Single Responsibility
content: The Single Responsibility Principle holds that a module should have one reason to change. A modal component has one responsibility: implementing a modal. Its markup, styles, and state all change for that same reason; splitting them across files fragments one responsibility rather than separating distinct ones.

title: Reusability
content: Co-location improves reuse because consumers import or discover a single .marko tag instead of coordinating separate HTML, CSS, and script files.

title: Component Size
content: When a component grows too large, the remedy is decomposing it into focused sub-components rather than splitting by file type: When styles alone become lengthy, auto-discovered adjacent stylesheets (style.css / <name>.style.css) still keep each component self-contained in its own folder.

title: Web Standards
content: Web standards define HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, not source-directory layouts. The platform itself supports co-location through Custom Elements, Shadow DOM, and inline <style> attributes.

title: Further Reading
content: Fine-Grained Bundling Nested Reactivity Optimizing Performance

title: Patch Protocol
content:
Patch Protocol [!TLDR] Navigations update the live page instead of loading a new document Client state, focus, and handlers survive, and the server sends only what changed Enabled per application with the patches option Experimental, coming soon A server-rendered page usually starts over on every navigation: the browser discards the document (along with every <let>, focused field, and scroll position), then parses and resumes a new one. Persisted pages, built on the patch protocol, keep the live document. When a link or form targets another route in the same application, the server renders that route as a patch: a stream of updates applied directly to the existing page. New structure is created from shells carried by the response, changed values are written in place, and untouched elements keep their client state. No HTML diffing happens on either side. Because the compiler knows every position where a server value can land, a patch writes values directly to those positions and leaves elements unrelated to server data alone. [!CAUTION]
The patch protocol is experimental and not available to try yet. The option, response format, and client runtime may change in any release, including patch releases. See Coming Soon in the August newsletter and the September update for progress so far.

title: Enabling
content: Pass patches: true to the Marko Run Vite plugin: This compiles every template to answer navigations with patches and installs the client router on each page.

title: Navigations
content: The router intercepts clicks on same-application links and submissions of GET or POST forms targeting same-application routes. Navigations fall through to the browser when targeting another origin or window, when a modifier key is held, on download links, on same-page fragment links, or when rel="external" is set. A handled navigation sends the same URL, method, and body the browser would send and applies the response as it streams: The document title and the route's +meta update with the page. A POST that redirects applies the target page and updates history to the final URL. Back and forward restore the visited entry's scroll position; new entries start at the top or at the target fragment. Repeated submissions of the same form while the first request is in flight are ignored. Whenever a response cannot apply as a patch (a non-patch response, a network failure, or a page loaded from an earlier build), the router falls back to a full document navigation so every navigation lands on the server-rendered page. Special pages such as +404 and +500 render as patches like any other route.

title: Shared Layouts
content: A layout keeps its client state while the nested page changes. Consider a shop with a cart drawer in the root layout: With the drawer open, navigating to /about replaces the page inside <main> and updates the cart count from the server response while cartOpen stays true because the layout is patched in place.

title: Client State
content: A component rendered in the same position before and after a navigation preserves its <let> values, typed field text, and script-attached DOM state: Submitting the form patches in the new results while keeping the filter panel open and the search input text intact. Because the <input> has no valueChange= handler, user edits stay untouched.

title: Scripts and Effects
content: Effects follow standard browser rendering rules: a <script> runs when its content mounts, re-runs when a referenced reactive value changes, and aborts $signal before each rerun and on removal. Content created by a patch runs its effects once the patch applies. Because patched markup is created on the client, an inline <html-script> inside newly inserted markup is added to the DOM without executing.

title: Content Security Policy
content: The client evaluates patch chunks as JavaScript. Pages served with a Content Security Policy require 'unsafe-eval' in script-src for patch navigations; without it, navigations fall back to full document loads.

title: Supported Pages
content: Patches apply to Tags API pages rendered through Marko Run route files. Templates rendered outside Marko Run (such as embedded templates) navigate with full document loads.

title: Page Size
content: Every page built with patches: true includes the client router, the used subset of the patch runtime, and HTML markers for patchable positions, making the initial document larger than a non-patched build. Subsequent patch responses are smaller than full documents because client-owned state is omitted and previously sent DOM shells are reused.

title: Optimizing Performance
content: Optimizing Performance [!TLDR] Run production builds with NODE_ENV=production so Marko strips debug checks and shortens internal IDs Pass promises into <await> rather than awaiting upstream to preserve streaming Keep reactive state narrow and lazy-load heavy below-the-fold widgets Marko's compiler applies streaming, fine-grained bundling, and compile-time reactivity automatically, so most templates are fast by default. When profiling reveals bottlenecks, focus on build configuration, async boundaries, client bundle scope, and serialized resume payloads.

title: Production Mode
content: Ensure production builds compile with NODE_ENV=production (or optimize: true in @marko/compiler). Production mode switches templates from the debug runtime to the optimized runtime, drops MARKO_DEBUG checks, and shortens internal template and scope identifiers.

title: Promise Passing
content: Start independent data fetches in parallel and pass their promises directly into <await> tags rather than awaiting them before rendering. Awaiting in a route handler or middleware holds back the entire HTML response, forfeiting streaming for static markup and <head> assets. See Promises over Awaiting.

title: Client Bundle Size
content: Because Marko bundles only interactive expressions, client JavaScript grows only with client-side state: Use the narrowest variable declaration that fits: static const for constants shared across instances, <const> for derived values, and <let> only for mutable state (see <let> vs <const>). Choose <show> when toggling bulky static markup that is already server-rendered so the browser does not bundle template creation code just to toggle visibility; choose <if> when hidden branches should not render on the server. Defer heavy interactive components (charts, rich editors, below-the-fold widgets) with lazy loading (with { load: "visible..." } or with { load: "idle" }).

title: Reducing Hydration Data
content: Marko serializes only the values read by browser code, embedded inline in the HTML for resumability. Keeping reactive state lean shrinks both HTML transfer size and browser parse time: Pass only the fields a client interaction actually reads rather than whole database records into interactive tags or event handlers. Keep server-only values out of $global.serializedGlobals. See Serializable State for how shared references and streaming flushes serialize.

title: Profiling
content: On the server, profile template throughput with Node's --cpu-prof flag or the Node Inspector under NODE_ENV=production to separate rendering cost from upstream I/O latency. In the browser, inspect bundle composition with Vite's bundle visualizer, view compiled client output in the Playground ("Client JS" tab), and measure interaction cost in browser DevTools.

title: Nested Reactivity
content: Nested Reactivity [!TLDR] Keep state local to the loop item or child component whenever outer code does not read it Hoist nested state into a parent collection only when ancestor UI depends on it Use immutable updates (or a helper like Immer) to propagate hoisted changes cleanly Applications frequently render collections where individual items have interactive state. Keeping that state as close to its usage as possible minimizes complexity and update work; hoist it into a parent collection only when surrounding UI needs to read or coordinate across items.

title: Local State
content: State should stay local whenever no ancestor needs to read it. For example, disabling each item's delete button until its checkbox is checked only concerns that single <li>: Because done lives inside the <for> body and the loop is keyed with by="id", toggling one checkbox updates only that row without touching the todos array.

title: Hoisted State
content: Hoist item state into the parent array when sibling or ancestor UI depends on it, such as displaying the next unfinished task outside the list: Replacing the updated item immutably with toSpliced keeps todos immutable so nextTodo recomputes automatically while by="id" preserves every row's DOM. For deeply nested structures where manual copying becomes verbose, an immutable update helper such as Immer integrates directly inside valueChange:

title: <let> vs <const>
content: <let> vs <const> [!TLDR] <let>: mutable reactive state <const>: derived value, pure, recomputes with dependencies static const: module-level constant, initialized once, not reactive A .marko template has three ways to bind a variable, each signaling how the value updates: <let> holds mutable state whose reassignment triggers reactive updates, <const> computes a derived value whenever its dependencies change, and static const evaluates once at module load for values that never vary across instances.

title: Mutable State
content: <let> declares state written directly, typically from event handlers. Assigning to its tag variable updates every expression that reads it: Clicking a button reassigns tipPercent, updating only the <output> text. The value= attribute sets only the initial value. Afterward, an uncontrolled <let> changes solely through assignment (or a valueChange handler), even if the initializing expression updates.

title: Derived Values
content:
<const> computes a value from other reactive variables. It cannot be reassigned and recomputes automatically whenever its dependencies change: tip always stays in sync with bill and tipPercent from a single declaration. [!WARNING]
Mirroring a derivation into a <let> and updating it manually is an anti-pattern: Every handler touching bill or tipPercent would have to recompute tip or leave it stale. Because updates are batched, a derived <const> read inside an event handler reflects the previous state until the queue flushes. See Stale Derived Values.

title: Module Constants
content:
Statements prefixed with static execute in module scope once per environment when the template loads, shared across every instance and request: currencyFormat is constructed once regardless of how many components render, making static const ideal for formatters, lookup tables, configuration, and helper functions. Static statements sit outside the reactive system; anything reading input or a tag variable belongs in <const> or <let>. [!NOTE]
Even a value that never changes after mount must use <const> if it reads input or a tag variable, so it initializes per instance.

title: Choosing
content: Choose the narrowest declaration that fits the value: Reassigned by handlers or mutable over time: <let> Computed from input or other reactive values: <const> Shared identically across every instance: static const Beyond clarity, targeted compilation generates browser update code only for values that can change, so narrower declarations produce less client work.

title: Immutable Data in State
content: Immutable Data in State [!TLDR] Replacing values rather than mutating them triggers reactive updates reliably Immutable state keeps rendered output a pure function of inputs and state Plain serializable values enable server-to-client resumability Marko's assignment-based reactivity expects state to be updated immutably with plain, serializable data. Treating rendered output as a deterministic function of inputs and state eliminates hidden side effects and keeps server-to-client handoff straightforward.

title: Immutability
content:
Marko detects changes when a <let> tag variable is reassigned and checked by reference equality (===). Creating a new array or object makes each state change explicit and triggers dependent DOM updates: [!WARNING]
Mutating an existing object or array in place (such as items.push("gamma") or user.clicks++) keeps the same reference and does not trigger a reactive update.

title: Functional UI
content: Because every update replaces the state reference rather than mutating fields behind the scenes, any expression reading that state always reflects a consistent snapshot:

title: Serialization
content: Resuming server-rendered HTML in the browser requires serializing any state that client code reads. Keeping state as plain objects, arrays, and supported built-ins rather than custom class instances or DOM nodes ensures reliable server-to-client transfer. See Serializable State for the full list of supported types.

title: Fine-Grained Bundling
content: Fine-Grained Bundling [!TLDR] Marko analyzes templates at compile time to bundle only interactive JavaScript Static markup ships zero client-side JavaScript Bundle size scales with interactivity rather than component boundaries Marko uses compile-time analysis to determine which expressions in a template can change in the browser. Static markup renders on the server and ships zero client JavaScript, so browser bundles contain only the code required for interactive behavior.

title: Beyond Islands
content: Islands architectures reduce client JavaScript at the component boundary, requiring explicit separation between server components and client components. Marko analyzes reactivity at the expression level across the state graph. Consider a product card containing a single interactive toggle: Only the click listener, watching state, and button text update ship to the browser. Code for rendering the heading, wrapping <div>, and static content stays on the server.

title: Architecture Independence
content: Because the compiler traces reactivity across component boundaries, splitting one template into many small components (or combining several into one) produces the same browser bundle size. Component boundaries follow separation of concerns without imposing hydration or bundle penalties. When interactive JavaScript itself should wait until needed (such as for a heavy below-the-fold widget), tags can be lazily loaded into separate bundles with declarative triggers.

title: Controllable Components
content: Controllable Components [!TLDR] Controlled components take their state from parent input props Uncontrolled components manage internal state directly Controllable components default to uncontrolled and become controlled when given a change handler Native tags and <let> implement this pattern via change handlers, with optional := shorthand Component authors rarely know in advance whether every caller will want to hoist state or leave it internal. Rather than forcing a permanent choice between controlled and uncontrolled APIs, Marko makes controllability a first-class language pattern.

title: Uncontrolled Components
content: An uncontrolled component owns its state internally through <let>: Because count lives inside counter.marko, callers use <counter/> with zero boilerplate, but a parent cannot read or reset count externally.

title: State Synchronization
content:
A common workaround is keeping internal state in <counter> while notifying the parent through an event callback: [!WARNING]
Mirroring child state into parent state is an anti-pattern. Prefer the controllable pattern so only one source of truth exists. This creates two count variables that must be kept in sync manually and can drift whenever either side changes independently.

title: Controlled Components
content: A controlled component delegates state ownership entirely to its parent: The parent has full control, but every caller must now allocate state and pass a countChange callback even when it never reads count.

title: The Controllable Pattern
content: A controllable component behaves as uncontrolled by default and switches to controlled whenever the caller supplies a <prop>Change handler.

title: Controllable Native Tags
content: Stateful HTML elements follow this exact model in Marko via change handlers. Adding valueChange= hands ownership of an <input> to Marko state, and the binding shorthand := writes both attributes together:

title: Controllable <let>
content: <let> is itself controllable. Binding it to input.count with := (shorthand for <let/count=input.count valueChange=input.countChange>) makes <counter> work in both modes: When countChange is a function (passed explicitly or via :=), <let> delegates updates to countChange and reflects input.count. When countChange is undefined, <let> manages local state initialized from input.count. title: Class to Tags API
content: Class to Tags API [!TLDR] Component boundaries carry no state or lifecycle overhead; state lives locally class, state, out, component, and instance methods have been removed input.renderBody is replaced by input.content Event handlers are standard function attributes rather than string-named methods Marko 4 and 5 used a Class API where each component file managed its own class, state, and lifecycle methods. Marko 6 replaces this with the Tags API, where state, reactivity, and side effects are declared inline as tags and analyzed at compile time.

title: Components Melt Away
content: In the Class API, state and lifecycle attach to component boundaries (state, onInput, onMount, onDestroy). In the Tags API, component boundaries serve code organization only: state lives locally in tag variables anywhere in the template (including inside conditionals and loops), and side effects attach to individual tags. Instance-lookup patterns like getComponent have been removed in favor of declarative data flow and exposed return values.

title: Updated APIs
content: Every removed Class API feature maps to a direct Tags API equivalent: out is replaced by $global for render-scoped globals class, state, and component are replaced by tag variables input.renderBody is renamed to input.content Instance methods map to declarative equivalents: getEl/getEls → native tag variables, getComponent → <return>, forceUpdate → reassigning <let>, subscribeTo → <script> with $signal Update directives (:scoped, :no-update, no-update, no-update-if, no-update-body, no-update-body-if) are no longer necessary because compiled updates are expression-level replaceState and setStateDirty are replaced by immutable <let> reassignment Split components are no longer necessary because targeted compilation splits static and interactive code automatically at the sub-template level

title: Event Handling
content: Attribute arguments such as onClick("handleClick") have been removed. Event handlers are standard function attributes written inline or passed by reference: Because event handlers are plain functions, they can be spread, wrapped, and called directly, replacing this.emit: Pass values back to a parent through standard function parameters:

content:
<script> runs browser side effects after mount and re-runs whenever referenced reactive values change, cleaning up through $signal: [!CAUTION]
Like React's useEffect, reserve <script> for synchronizing with external side effects; prefer <const> and <let> for derived values and state.
